1.note: David is speaking of the temple where Yahweh is worshiped as if it were a **house** in which he lived. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the temple of Yahweh]

2.note: Here David is using one part of their bodies, their **feet**, to mean all of them in the act of standing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [We are standing]

David is speaking to **Jerusalem**, which is a city that cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him how he feels about Jerusalem. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about Jerusalem. Alternate translation: [within the gates of Jerusalem]

Here the word **gates** refers to the entire city or town. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [within you, the city of]

3.note: The point of this comparison is that just as a city whose parts are **joined** together is compact and unified, so is Jerusalem well-constructed and cohesive. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [so that all its parts are compact and unified]

The expression **is joined** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [that holds itself together]

4.note: David is using this possessive form to mean that the tribes belong to and worship Yahweh because he is their God. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the tribes that worship Yahweh]
The word **Yah** is a shortened form of the name “Yahweh,” the God of Israel. You could use the full name if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **testimony**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [as Yahweh instructed the people of Israel to do]

Here, **to** marks **give thanks to the name of Yahweh** as the goal or purpose of the tribes going up. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [so that they can give thanks to the name of Yahweh]

David is using the term **name** to represent who Yahweh is or to refer to Yahweh himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to Yahweh himself]

5.note: Here, **For** introduces the reason why the tribes go up to Jerusalem: it is the place where kings will sit on their thrones to render justice. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason. Alternate translation: [Because that is where kings sit on thrones for judgment]

Here, **thrones** represents the kings’ royal authority to rule and judge. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [kings to carry out their judicial authority]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **judgment**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [where kings are judging]

David is leaving out words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [there sit thrones for the house of David]

Here, **house** means all the people descended from a particular person. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. So **the house of David** figuratively means all the people descended from David. Alternate translation: [for the descendants of David]

6.note: David is using words with similar sounds for poetic effect. In the original language, the words for **ask**, **peace**, and **prosper** all share sounds similar to the word for **Jerusalem**. David is using this wordplay to connect his prayer for the city with its very name. You may want to reproduce this effect if poetry in your language does this. If not, you could indicate it in a footnote.

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **peace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Ask that those in the city of Jerusalem may live peacefully]
Here the name **Jerusalem** represents the people who live in that city. Alternate translation: [those who live in Jerusalem]

In this verse and to the end of the psalm, David is again speaking to Jerusalem, which is a city that cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about the welfare of those who love the city. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about Jerusalem. Alternate translation: [may the ones loving Jerusalem prosper]

David is saying what he wants to happen. See the discussion in the introduction to Psalms about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [I pray that the ones loving you will prosper]

7.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the ideas of **peace** and **prosperity**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [May people live peacefully within your rampart, prosperously in your citadels]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. David uses the two phrases together to emphasize his desire for the well-being of Jerusalem. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way, as the UST does. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [Let there be peace within your rampart, yes, let there be prosperity in your citadels]

David is asking Yahweh to bless the people of Israel. In your translation, use a form that people would recognize as a blessing in your language. You might express this as a prayer, if that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [May Yahweh bring peace]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [let there be prosperity]

8.note: Here, **For** marks **the sake of my brothers and my companions** as the motivation for David speaking peace. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [Because I love my brothers and my companions]

The psalmist is using the term **brothers** to describe people who are descended from the same ancestor or all the Israelites. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my countrymen]

David is using **please, peace in you** as a common expression of his culture used to wish someone well or to pronounce a blessing. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [let me say, “Peace be with you”] or [I pray for peace for you]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **peace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [may people live peacefully within you]

9.note: Here, **For** marks **the sake of the house of Yahweh our God** as the motivation for David seeking good. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [Because I love the house of Yahweh our God]

David is speaking of the temple where Yahweh is worshiped as if it were a **house** in which he lived. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the temple of Yahweh]
David is using the adjective **good** as a noun to refer to good things. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression. Alternate translation: [what is good]
